title: Hearing Dizzy, Parker's music too modern, head arrangements
summary: He heard Dizzy at the Onyx, found Parker too modern for most, and worked up small head arrangements with him.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Had you heard Dizzy before you played with Charlie Parker?
Oh yeah, he played across the street at the Onyx I think, with Don Byas.
Did you hear Dizzy when you first get to New York at Monroe's or Minton's.
...I can't remember... I remember Joe Guy a lot.
To you recall about Parker's music, did it seem very modern.
That's the thing, it was too modern, you know

And it hurt him for quite a while cause he couldn't get nobody to understand it, except me, and I couldn't do anything about it. I'd tell guys. The guys used to flock around to hear us play, and listen to him. I just let him play. I was proud because he was one of the few cats -- a lot of cats come in and you're glad to get rid of 'em. He came around every night. He was a good guy, boy, I'll tell you. Nothin' wrong with him. He was a hell of a nice guy man. What he went into, I got nothin' to do with that. But otherwise, his personality, as being a human being, he couldn't be beat. No problem, no arguments, no nothin'. He was glad to play, and I played everything that I could back him up doing. Then we played a few things together. And little arrangements started coming out and things.

This was when he sat in because he came around so often naturally, that's how all arrangements were made at that particular time -- small groups -- called head arrangements; which means you had to remember what you did, keep puttin' it together in your head a little more, and sounds as if someone wrote you an arrangement in music, but it's really from the brain.
Then here come this fella Lubinsky, Herman Lubinsky. He and his short self with his beard.
